name: Six Thinking Hats
description: Edward de Bono's parallel thinking method (1985) for structured group and individual deliberation. Six colored hats represent six directions of thought: Blue (managing), White (facts), Red (emotions), Black (caution), Yellow (optimism), Green (creativity). All participants 'wear' the same hat simultaneously — parallel thinking replaces adversarial debate by having everyone explore the same direction together before moving to the next. Hat sequences always begin and end with Blue (the facilitator hat). Programs are often 'emergent': the facilitator plans the first few hats, then adjusts based on what the discussion needs. Example sequences from de Bono: Initial Ideas (Blue→White→Green→Blue), Choosing Between Alternatives (Blue→White→Green→Yellow→Black→Red→Blue), Solving Problems (Blue→White→Green→Red→Yellow→Black→Green→Blue). Each hat lasts ~2 minutes; Red is ~30 seconds (visceral gut reaction). This default program uses: Blue (opening) → White → Red → Yellow → Black → Green → Blue (closing).

steps.name: 🔵 Blue Hat (Opening) — The Big Picture & Managing
steps.description:
SEQUENTIAL THINKING REQUIRED

The Blue Hat opens every Six Thinking Hats session. It is the facilitator's hat — 'The Big Picture' — responsible for managing the thinking process itself, not the subject.

Using the CAF (Consider All Factors) technique, define:
• What is the subject or problem under discussion?
• What are the goals of this thinking session?
• Which hat sequence will be used? (Default: White → Red → Yellow → Black → Green → Blue closing. Adjust if the problem suggests a different program — e.g., 'Identifying Solutions' uses Blue→White→Black→Green→Blue.)
• What time constraints apply?

Per de Bono: 'The key to a successful use of the Six Thinking Hats methodology was the deliberate focusing of the discussion on a particular approach as needed.' The Blue Hat sets this focus.

Note: Programs are often 'emergent' — plan the first few hats, then the facilitator sees what seems to be the right way to go.

SequentialThinking.reason: Frame the problem using CAF (Consider All Factors) and determine the hat sequence program
focus_areas: Define the subject, scope, and goals of this thinking session
Choose the hat sequence program (or confirm the default)
Identify any constraints: time, information gaps, stakeholders

SearchMemories.reason: Gather prior context, decisions, and related thinking sessions to frame the problem accurately

stop_conditions: Subject and goals of the thinking session clearly defined
Hat sequence program chosen (default or adapted for the problem type)
Constraints and success criteria stated
All participants aligned on the process
next_actions: Proceed to White Hat for objective facts and information gathering

steps.name: ⚪ White Hat — Facts & Information
steps.description:
The White Hat focuses exclusively on objective facts, data, and information. No interpretation, no opinions, no argument.

Per de Bono, the White Hat direction is 'Facts & Information' using the technique of information gathering. Ask:
• What data do we have? What data do we need?
• What are the known facts relevant to this subject?
• What information is missing? Where can we find it?
• What are the trends in the data?

Critical discipline: separate facts from inferences. 'Believed facts' and 'checked facts' should be distinguished. When a participant offers an opinion disguised as a fact, the facilitator redirects: 'That's a Red Hat or Black Hat contribution — we're wearing White Hat right now.'

This hat typically runs ~2 minutes.

SearchMemories.reason: Retrieve objective facts, prior data, and documented knowledge from the knowledge graph

BuildContext.reason: Map the factual landscape — concepts, relationships, and data points relevant to the subject

stop_conditions: Known facts catalogued without interpretation or opinion
Data sources identified and credibility noted (checked vs. believed facts)
Information gaps explicitly stated — what we need but don't have
No Black/Red/Yellow contributions mixed in — pure information
next_actions: Proceed to Red Hat for emotional reactions and gut feelings

steps.name: 🔴 Red Hat — Feelings & Emotions
steps.description:
SEQUENTIAL THINKING REQUIRED

The Red Hat permits the expression of emotions, feelings, hunches, and intuitions — without any need for justification or logical explanation. De Bono's technique here is 'Emotions and Ego' with a recommended duration of ~30 seconds of visceral gut reaction.

Rules:
• No justification required — 'I just don't like it' is a valid Red Hat statement.
• Capture immediate emotional response before rationalisation sets in.
• In group settings, this is often done via anonymous dot-voting to surface honest reactions.
• The Red Hat legitimises emotions in a thinking process that might otherwise suppress them.

Ask:
• What is your gut feeling about this?
• What emotional reactions does this subject provoke?
• What hunches or intuitions arise — even if you can't explain them?

Keep this step brief and visceral. Lengthy justification belongs under Black or Yellow Hat, not Red.

SequentialThinking.reason: Surface instinctive gut reactions — de Bono recommends ~30 seconds of visceral response with no justification
focus_areas: Immediate emotional response — what does your gut say?
Hunches and intuitions — even unexplainable ones

stop_conditions: Gut reactions recorded without rational justification
Emotional responses from relevant stakeholder perspectives captured
Hunches and intuitions explicitly stated, even if unexplainable
Step kept brief (~30 seconds equivalent) — no extended rationalisation
next_actions: Proceed to Yellow Hat for benefits and optimistic assessment

steps.name: 🟡 Yellow Hat — Positive & Optimistic
steps.description:
The Yellow Hat explores benefits, value, and optimistic possibilities. It uses the PMI technique (focusing on the Plus dimension) to systematically identify what is good about an idea.

Per de Bono, the Yellow Hat direction is 'Positive' — not naive optimism, but a deliberate effort to find value and merit even in ideas that seem weak. Ask:
• What are the benefits?
• What is the best-case outcome?
• What value does this create and for whom?
• Why might this work? What supporting evidence exists?
• What are the long-term positive consequences?

The Yellow Hat requires effort — it is often harder to be constructive than critical. Unlike Black Hat thinking (which comes naturally to many people), Yellow Hat thinking must be deliberate and disciplined.

This hat typically runs ~2 minutes.

SearchMemories.reason: Find supporting evidence, precedents, and positive outcomes from the knowledge graph

stop_conditions: Benefits and value propositions documented with supporting logic
Best-case outcomes identified and articulated
PMI Plus dimension explored — deliberate effort to find merit
Long-term positive consequences considered
next_actions: Proceed to Black Hat for critical evaluation and risk assessment

steps.name: ⚫ Black Hat — Caution & Critical Judgment
steps.description:
SEQUENTIAL THINKING REQUIRED

The Black Hat is for critical judgment and caution. It uses PMI (focusing on the Minus and Interesting dimensions) and systematic evaluation to identify risks, problems, and weaknesses.

Per de Bono, the Black Hat direction is 'Negative / Critical' — it is the hat of logical caution. This is NOT adversarial attack or ego-driven criticism. It is disciplined, objective risk assessment:
• What could go wrong?
• What are the logical weaknesses in this proposal?
• Does this fit the facts (from White Hat)?
• What are the risks and their likelihood?
• What are the costs, obstacles, and difficulties?
• Where does this not fit experience or established principles?

De Bono notes that Black Hat thinking is the most used and arguably the most valuable hat — but it must be kept in its place. When criticism dominates, it kills creative ideas (Green Hat) before they can be developed.

SequentialThinking.reason: Systematic risk analysis using PMI (Minus and Interesting dimensions) and logical evaluation
focus_areas: Risks, failure modes, and their likelihood
Logical weaknesses and flaws in the proposal
Costs, obstacles, and difficulties — does this fit the facts from White Hat?

stop_conditions: All significant risks and problems identified with likelihood assessment
Logical weaknesses and flaws in proposals exposed
Costs and obstacles documented
Criticism is logical and objective — not adversarial or ego-driven
next_actions: Proceed to Green Hat for creative thinking and new ideas

steps.name: 🟢 Green Hat — New Ideas & Creative Thinking
steps.description:
SEQUENTIAL THINKING REQUIRED

The Green Hat is for creativity, new ideas, and alternatives. It uses de Bono's Concept Challenge technique and the lateral thinking provocation 'Po' (Yes, No, Po) to escape established patterns.

Per de Bono, the Green Hat direction is 'New Ideas' — it is not about judging ideas (that's Black/Yellow) but about generating them. Rules:
• Suspend judgment — all ideas are welcome, even absurd ones.
• Use 'Po' provocations: deliberately unreasonable statements that force new thinking directions (e.g., 'Po: what if we did the exact opposite?').
• Apply Concept Challenge: question why things are done this way — not because they're wrong, but to open up alternatives.
• Seek movement value, not truth value — where does an idea lead, not whether it's correct?

Ask:
• What alternatives exist beyond what we've discussed?
• What creative or unconventional approaches might work?
• What would a completely different perspective suggest?
• What new ideas emerge from combining or modifying existing ones?

This hat typically runs ~2 minutes.

SequentialThinking.reason: Divergent idea generation using Concept Challenge and lateral thinking provocations (de Bono's 'Po')
focus_areas: Generate novel alternatives beyond conventional thinking
Apply at least one 'Po' provocation to escape established patterns
Concept Challenge: question why current approaches exist — seek movement value

stop_conditions: Novel alternatives generated beyond conventional thinking
At least one 'Po' provocation explored for movement value
Concept Challenge applied — assumptions about current approach questioned
Creative ideas documented without premature judgment (no Black Hat here)
next_actions: Proceed to Blue Hat (closing) for synthesis and action planning

steps.name: 🔵 Blue Hat (Closing) — Synthesis & Next Steps
steps.description:
The Blue Hat closes every Six Thinking Hats session, just as it opened it. The closing Blue Hat synthesizes all perspectives into a coherent outcome using FIP (First Important Priorities).

Responsibilities:
• Summarise what was learned from each hat:
  — White: key facts and information gaps
  — Red: dominant emotional responses and intuitions
  — Yellow: main benefits and opportunities
  — Black: critical risks and weaknesses
  — Green: most promising creative ideas and alternatives
• Apply FIP (First Important Priorities) to rank findings by importance.
• Identify decisions that can be made now vs. those needing more information.
• Define concrete next steps and action items.
• Note whether the session achieved its goals (set in the opening Blue Hat).
• If unresolved tensions remain, recommend a follow-up session with a tailored hat sequence.

Per de Bono: 'Six Thinking Hats and the associated idea of parallel thinking provide a means for groups to plan thinking processes in a detailed and cohesive way, and in doing so to think together more effectively.'

WriteMemory.reason: Document synthesized findings, FIP-ranked priorities, and action items as institutional memory

stop_conditions: All hat perspectives synthesized into a coherent summary
Priorities ranked using FIP (First Important Priorities)
Concrete next steps and action items defined
Session goals (from opening Blue Hat) assessed — achieved or unresolved
Follow-up session recommended if tensions remain unresolved
next_actions: Workflow complete — deliver synthesized analysis with FIP-ranked priorities
